title: Trip state machine
idea: A trip state machine is the fixed set of trip statuses plus the only legal moves between them, enforced in one place.
points: Statuses are an `enum`; each constant answers `canMoveTo(next)` with a `switch` expression.
Every event method calls one private `moveTo`, which rejects illegal moves with `IllegalStateException`.
Cancel is legal only before pickup; `COMPLETED` and `CANCELLED` are terminal, with no exits.
Driver apps resend events; `synchronized` methods keep check-then-set atomic per trip.

steps.caption: A new `Trip` starts in `REQUESTED`. The constructor records it as the first history entry.
`assign` is legal only from `REQUESTED`. The driver id is stored after the move succeeds.
`arrive` then `start` follow the happy path. Each one is a single allowed arrow.
`complete` needs a positive fare and is legal only from `IN_PROGRESS`.
Cancel arrows leave only the three pre-pickup states. Mid-ride, the only exit is `complete`.
Terminal states have no outgoing arrows. A late `start` or `assign` is rejected, not applied.

code.title: The problem: a status string
code.caption: A free-form setter accepts any status in any order, so money and history go wrong silently.

walk.text: The setter checks nothing: not the value, not the current state, not the caller.
A buggy driver app jumps to `COMPLETED`, so the rider pays for a ride that never started.
A typo becomes a new status, and the trip is cancelled after the charge.
A retried message moves a running trip back to `REQUESTED`. Matching could send a second driver.
Business rules test raw strings scattered through the code. Each new rule is another place to get wrong.

code.title: The fix: enum transitions
code.caption: One enum owns the legal moves; the trip exposes events, never a raw setter.

walk.text: An `enum` makes typos impossible: an unknown status no longer compiles.
The whole transition table in one `switch`. The compiler forces a case for every constant.
Events validate input first, move second, and change other fields only after the move succeeds.
The single gate: an illegal move throws with trip id, from and to, and changes nothing.
`synchronized` stops two duplicate events on one trip from both passing the check.
Cancel mid-ride and a stale reassign are both refused; the history shows they never happened.

pitfalls: A public `setStatus` lets callers bypass every rule; expose events like `start()` instead.
Updating `driverId` before `moveTo` leaves a half-changed trip when the move is rejected.
Silently ignoring an illegal event hides app bugs; throw, or log and return the current status.

quiz.q: Same classes as the fix. What does the last line print?
options: T-3 D1 [REQUESTED, ASSIGNED, CANCELLED, ARRIVED] fare=0
quiz.why: Cancel from `ASSIGNED` is legal. `CANCELLED` is terminal, so `arrive` throws before touching history, and `attempt` prints the error.

takeaway: Statuses in an enum, moves in one gate, events instead of setters.

starters: Should I use the State pattern with one class per status instead of an enum?
How do I persist the trip status safely when two servers handle events?
Where should side effects like charging the rider run after a transition?
